<reason>This was a close, high-quality exchange. Side B's core move — reading the motion's purpose clause so that donor-egg IVF already "prevents the disease," leaving MRT to purchase only relatedness plus reversion risk — was sharp and well-executed, and B's pressure question forcing A to concede "the disease outcome is the same" was the debate's best trap. But Side A assembled two responses B never fully neutralized: (1) the empirical precedent that public systems already fund IVF with PGD precisely to secure genetically related healthy children, so the "state never pays for lineage" premise fails, and B's "PGD is rationed too" reply concedes funding and becomes an argument about how, not whether; and (2) the homoplasmic/high-load cohort, where PGD offers nothing and B's comparator collapses into "donation only," leaving the live choice as tracked small risk versus near-certain untracked natural transmission — a comparison B relabeled rather than answered. B's kind-distinction (PGD failure means no pregnancy; MRT failure means a sick child who transmits) was genuinely forceful and kept the safety route alive, and the "trial vs routine service" framing landed, but A's staged, registry-governed funding pathway is a defensible reading of what the motion asks. Narrow edge to A on the surviving comparator and the unanswered natural-conception counterfactual.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Pressure Q1 ("name one disease outcome MRT delivers that donation does not") forced A's concession that the disease outcome is identical, which B weaponized across Rebuttal 2 and the Closing — the sharpest single exchange. A's most decisive reply was the PGD precedent plus the homoplasmic access gap in Rebuttal 2 [A4.1–A4.5], showing the state already funds related-healthy-child goals and that B's comparator fails exactly the families at the heart of the motion.</best_rebuttal>
